title: Open Globe Injury: Rupture & Reconstruction
summary: Rupture of the globe is a vision-threatening emergency defined by a full-thickness wound of the eye wall caused by blunt trauma. Rapid diagnosis, protective measures, and primary surgical closure are the cornerstones of management to prevent irreversible blindness and sympathetic ophthalmia.

sections.title: Etiology & Pathophysiology
sections.content: Rupture occurs when blunt force causes a sudden increase in intraocular pressure (IOP). The eye wall gives way at its weakest points: the limbus, the insertion of the rectus muscles (where the sclera is thinnest at ~0.3mm), and prior surgical incisions (e.g., old ECCE scars). This is an 'inside-out' injury mechanism compared to the 'outside-in' nature of sharp lacerations.

rows: High risk of RD and severe vision loss

sections.title: Clinical Features & Signs
content: Marked vision loss (often NLP to HM)
Severe subconjunctival hemorrhage (often bullous/360°)
Shallow or extremely deep Anterior Chamber
Peaked or 'teardrop' pupil pointing toward the wound
Iris prolapse (brown uveal tissue at wound)
Hyphema (often total/8-ball)
Vitreous hemorrhage
Commotio retinae or retinal detachment

sections.title: The 'Occult' Rupture Red Flags
content: 360-degree Bullous Subconjunctival Hemorrhage (high suspicion for scleral rupture)
Persistent hypotony (IOP < 5 mmHg) after blunt trauma
Abnormally deep anterior chamber (posterior rupture)
Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD)
Limitation of ocular motility (muscle involvement or incarceration)

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Imaging
content: Step 1: History (time, mechanism, last meal for NPO)
Step 2: Visual Acuity (crucial for OTS scoring)
Step 3: External exam (DO NOT perform tonometry or push on globe)
Step 4: Non-contrast CT Orbits (1mm thin cuts) to look for 'Flat Tire Sign'
Step 5: B-Scan Ultrasound (ONLY if globe is closed/repaired; contraindicated in open globe)

rows: IOP may be high, globe intact

sections.title: Immediate Management Protocol
content: 1. Apply rigid Fox Shield (no pressure patches)
2. Bed rest with head elevated 30 degrees
3. NPO status for urgent surgical repair
4. IV Antibiotics: Vancomycin (1g Q12h) + Ceftazidime (1g Q12h) or Ciprofloxacin
5. Update Tetanus prophylaxis
6. Analgesics and Anti-emetics (Ondansetron) to prevent Valsalva

sections.title: Surgical Repair Principles
content: General Anesthesia (avoid succinylcholine - increases IOP)
360-degree peritomy to explore all quadrants
Primary goal: Restore globe integrity (water-tight closure)
Minimize tissue excision (repose viable uveal tissue)
Corneal Scleral wounds: Suture limbus first as anatomical landmark
'Close-as-you-go' technique for long scleral wounds

content.explanation: Bilateral granulomatous panuveitis following trauma to one eye (exciting eye). Occurs 2 weeks to many years later. Dalen-Fuchs nodules are characteristic.

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Suspect Endophthalmitis
content: Increasing pain out of proportion to injury
Rapidly decreasing vision post-repair
Increasing hypopyon or vitritis
Fibrinous anterior chamber reaction
Eyelid edema and chemosis worsening

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for the Resident
content: Always examine the fellow eye thoroughly; trauma is often the focus, but pre-existing conditions or bilateral trauma can be missed.
If the wound is posterior to the rectus insertions, do not attempt to excise prolapsed vitreous aggressively as it may cause more traction.
Low IOP is the most reliable sign of occult rupture, but a normal IOP does NOT rule it out.
The 'Flat Tire Sign' on CT refers to the loss of the globe's spherical contour.
Siderosis bulbi: Retained iron foreign bodies can cause irreversible retinal toxicity within weeks.
